**Summary of Regulation (EC) No 1393/2007**

This Regulation (EC) No 1393/2007 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on 13 November 2007, amends and replaces Regulation (EC) No 1348/2000 on the service in the Member States of judicial and extrajudicial documents in civil or commercial matters. It is a Regulation with legal basis in Article 61(c) and Article 67(5), second indent, of the Treaty establishing the European Community.

The Regulation applies to civil and commercial matters where judicial or extrajudicial documents must be transmitted between Member States for service. It does not apply to revenue, customs, administrative matters, or liability of the State (acta iure imperii), nor where the address of the person to be served is unknown. It also does not apply in cases involving persons whose address is not known, or where the document is not intended for service between Member States.

The Regulation establishes a general framework for the service of documents between Member States, including designation of transmitting and receiving agencies, procedures for transmission, receipt, service, refusal, and remedies. Key provisions include:

- Each Member State designates one or more transmitting and receiving agencies (which may be the same or different), with a five-year term renewable every five years.  
- Documents must be transmitted directly and as soon as possible; transmission may use any appropriate means, provided the content is true and legible.  
- The document must be accompanied by a request completed in the official language of the Member State addressed (or an official language of the place where service is to be effected, or another language accepted by the Member State).  
- Receiving agencies must serve the document within one month of receipt; if not possible within that period, they must inform the transmitting agency and continue efforts to effect service, unless the transmitting agency specifies a time limit after which service is no longer required.  
- The receiving agency must inform the addressee in writing, using the standard form set out in Annex II, that the addressee may refuse to accept the document or return it within one week if it is not in a language the addressee understands or in the official language or one of the official languages of the place of service. Refusal may be remedied by serving a translated copy of the document, with service date determined according to the law of the Member State addressed.  
- The date of service is the date on which the document is served in accordance with the law of the Member State addressed; where a Member State law requires service within a specific period, that period is used for the applicant’s reference date.  
- The service must be effected as soon as possible, within one month of receipt; if not possible within that time, the receiving agency must notify the transmitting agency and continue efforts, unless otherwise specified.  
- The Regulation applies to judicial and extrajudicial documents, and also covers other means of transmission and service, including consular/diplomatic channels, service by diplomatic or consular agents, service by postal services (e.g., registered letter with acknowledgement of receipt), and direct service by judicial officers or competent persons where permitted under national law.  
- Costs of service are not payable by the Member State; the applicant bears costs related to recourse to judicial officers or competent persons, which must be fixed in advance and respect proportionality and non-discrimination principles. Member States shall communicate such fixed fees to the Commission.  
- The Regulation applies to service of documents in civil and commercial matters only; it does not apply to service on authorized representatives in the Member State where proceedings are taking place, regardless of residence.  
- The Regulation repeals Regulation (EC) No 1348/2000 and supersedes it.  
- The Regulation prevails over bilateral or multilateral agreements or arrangements having the same scope, such as the Protocol annexed to the Brussels Convention of 27 September 1968 and the Hague Convention of 15 November 1965, unless the Member State maintains or concludes other agreements compatible with this Regulation.  
- Member States may maintain or conclude additional agreements or arrangements to expedite or simplify document transmission, provided they remain compatible with this Regulation.  
- Member States shall notify the Commission of the designation of agencies, their jurisdiction, means of receipt, and acceptable languages for standard forms (Annex I).  
- The Commission shall review the application of this Regulation no later than 1 June 2011, and every five years thereafter, and may propose amendments.  
- The Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 13 November 2008, with Article 23 (referring to refusal and service remedies) applying from 13 August 2008.  
- The Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in the Member States in accordance with the Treaty establishing the European Community.

Defined terms (as used in the Regulation):
- “Member State” – refers to all Member States except Denmark.
- “transmitting agency” – the public officer, authority, or other person designated by a Member State to transmit judicial or extrajudicial documents.
- “receiving agency” – the public officer, authority, or other person designated by a Member State to receive judicial or extrajudicial documents.
- “standard form” – the form set out in Annex I (for transmission and service procedures) and Annex II (for refusal notices).
- “service” – the act of delivering or attempting to deliver a document to the recipient in accordance with the law of the Member State where service is to be effected.
- “refusal” – the right of the addressee to refuse to accept a document or to return it within one week if it is not in an acceptable language.
- “date of service” – the date on which the document is served in accordance with the law of the Member State addressed; where a Member State law requires service within a specific period, that period is used for the applicant’s reference date.
- “official language” – the official language(s) of the Member State addressed or, where applicable, the official language or one of the official languages of the place where service is to be effected.

Obligations, prohibitions, and entitlements (as per articles):
- Obligations:
  - Member States must designate transmitting and receiving agencies, designate them for a five-year term renewable every five years, and notify the Commission of their details (Annex I).
  - Transmitting agencies must transmit documents directly and as soon as possible, using appropriate means, and accompany the document with a request completed in the official language or an acceptable language of the Member State addressed.
  - Receiving agencies must serve the document within one month of receipt; if not possible within that period, they must notify the transmitting agency and continue efforts to effect service, unless the transmitting agency specifies a time limit after which service is no longer required.
  - Receiving agencies must inform the addressee in writing using the standard form (Annex II) that the addressee may refuse to accept the document or return it within one week if the document is not in an acceptable language.
  - Receiving agencies must continue to take all necessary steps to effect service unless the transmitting agency specifies otherwise.
  - Member States must not allow service of a document on an authorized representative in the Member State where proceedings are taking place, regardless of residence.
  - The Regulation applies to judicial and extrajudicial documents in civil and commercial matters; it does not apply to revenue, customs, administrative matters, or acta iure imperii.
  - The Regulation applies from 13 November 2008 (with Article 23 applying from 13 August 2008).
  - Member States must communicate fixed fees for service to the Commission, as required by Article 11.
  - Member States may maintain or conclude additional agreements or arrangements compatible with this Regulation.
  - The Regulation repeals Regulation (EC) No 1348/2000.

Prohibitions:
- Member States may not apply the Regulation to service on authorized representatives in the Member State where proceedings are taking place, regardless of residence.
- The Regulation prohibits reliance on bilateral or multilateral agreements that conflict with its provisions, except where Member States maintain or conclude other compatible agreements.
- The Regulation does not permit Member States to maintain or conclude agreements that undermine the core obligations of this Regulation (e.g., by imposing incompatible service rules).
- No Member State may refuse to apply the standard forms or procedures set out in Annexes I and II.

Entitlements:
- Recipients (addressees) have the entitlement to refuse to accept a document if it is not in an acceptable language (as defined in Article 8), and to return it within one week; they may also be entitled to receive a translated copy of the document served, with service date determined according to the law of the Member State addressed.
- Transmitters have the entitlement to transmit documents directly and as soon as possible, using appropriate means, and to accompany them with a request in an acceptable language.
- Receiving agencies have the entitlement to serve the document within one month of receipt, and to continue efforts to effect service if not possible within that period, unless the transmitting agency specifies otherwise.
- The Regulation provides for remedies for refusal and for service delays, including the ability to serve a translated copy and to determine the applicable service date based on the Member State’s own legal rules.

REGULATION (EC) NO 300/2008  
OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL  
of 11 March 2008  
on common rules in the field of civil aviation security and repealing Regulation (EC) No 2320/2002  

(Text with EEA relevance)  

(1) Type and title: Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council  
(2) Legal basis in the Treaties: Article 80(2) of the Treaty establishing the European Community  

(3) Subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application:  
This Regulation establishes common rules to protect civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference that jeopardise the security of civil aviation, and provides a basis for a common interpretation of Annex 17 to the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation. It applies to:  
- All airports or parts of airports located in the territory of a Member State that are not exclusively used for military purposes;  
- All operators, including air carriers, providing services at such airports;  
- All entities applying aviation security standards that operate from premises inside or outside airport premises and provide goods and/or services to or through airports referred to above.  

Additionally, the Regulation covers security measures on board aircraft of Community air carriers, and applies to flights from Member State airports to, or over, third countries, subject to equivalence criteria and third‑country notification procedures. It does not apply to military airports or activities outside the scope of civil aviation.  

(4) Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- Member States must designate a single authority responsible for coordination and monitoring of the implementation of the common basic standards (Article 9).  
- Each Member State must draw up, apply and maintain a national civil aviation security programme (Article 10).  
- Every airport operator, air carrier and entity must draw up, apply and maintain an airport, air carrier or entity security programme that complies with the Regulation and the national programme (Articles 12, 13, 14).  
- Operators and entities must implement the common basic standards set out in Annex (Article 4).  
- Member States may apply more stringent measures than the common basic standards, provided they are based on a risk assessment and comply with Community law (Article 6).  
- The Commission may adopt general measures amending non‑essential elements of the common basic standards by supplementing them (Article 4(2) and Article 19(3)).  
- Member States shall inform the Commission of any more stringent measures they apply (Article 6).  
- The Commission shall conduct inspections (including unannounced inspections) to monitor compliance (Article 15).  
- Penalties may be imposed for infringements of the Regulation; they must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 21).  
- The Regulation repeals Regulation (EC) No 2320/2002 (Article 23).  

(5) Key defined terms (as defined in Article 3):  
- ‘civil aviation’ – any air operation carried out by civil aircraft, excluding State aircraft referred to in Article 3 of the Chicago Convention.  
- ‘aviation security’ – the combination of measures and resources intended to safeguard civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference that jeopardise security.  
- ‘operator’ – a person, organisation or enterprise engaged, or offering to engage, in an air transport operation.  
- ‘air carrier’ – an air transport undertaking holding a valid operating licence or equivalent.  
- ‘Community air carrier’ – an air carrier holding a valid operating licence granted by a Member State in accordance with Council Regulation (EEC) No 2407/92.  
- ‘entity’ – a person, organisation or enterprise other than an operator.  
- ‘prohibited articles’ – weapons, explosives or other dangerous devices, articles or substances that may be used to commit an act of unlawful interference that jeopardises security.  
- ‘screening’ – the application of technical or other means intended to identify and/or detect prohibited articles.  
- ‘security control’ – the application of means by which the introduction of prohibited articles may be prevented.  
- ‘access control’ – the application of means by which the entry of unauthorised persons or vehicles may be prevented.  
- ‘airside’ – the movement area of an airport, adjacent terrain and buildings or portions thereof, access to which is restricted.  
- ‘landside’ – those parts of an airport, adjacent terrain and buildings or portions thereof that are not airside.  
- ‘security restricted area’ – an area of airside where, in addition to access being restricted, other aviation security standards are applied.  
- ‘demarcated area’ – an area separated by means of access control from security restricted areas, or, if the demarcated area itself is a security restricted area, from other security restricted areas of an airport.  
- ‘background check’ – a recorded check of a person’s identity, including criminal history, as part of assessment of suitability for unescorted access to security restricted areas.  
- ‘in‑flight security officer’ – a person employed by a state to travel on an aircraft of an air carrier licensed by it, whose purpose is to protect that aircraft and its occupants against acts of unlawful interference.  

(6) Entry‑into‑force date and transitional / sunset provisions:  
- The Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (Article 24, paragraph 1).  
- It shall apply from the date specified in the implementing rules adopted in accordance with the procedures referred to in Article 4(2) and (3), but not later than 24 months after its entry into force (Article 24, paragraph 2).  
- Certain provisions (e.g., Articles 4(2), 4(3), 4(4), 8, 11(2), 15(1) second subparagraph, 17, 19 and 22) apply from the date of entry into force of the Regulation (Article 24, paragraph 3).  

The Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.

REGULATION (EC) No 763/2008  
of 9 July 2008  
on population and housing censuses  

(Text with EEA relevance)  

This Regulation establishes common rules for the decennial provision of comprehensive data on population and housing.  

The Regulation applies to all Member States and has a territorial, sectoral and personal scope covering population and housing statistics at national, regional (NUTS levels 1, 2 and 3; LAU level 2) and local levels, as defined in Annex.  

The primary obligations established are:  
- Member States shall submit to the Commission (Eurostat) data on population and housing characteristics at the defined geographical levels, including demographic, social, economic and housing data, as detailed in Annex, in accordance with Article 3.  
- Member States shall ensure that the data sources and methodology used meet, to the highest possible extent, the essential features of population and housing censuses (individual enumeration, simultaneity, universality within a defined territory, availability of small-area data and defined periodicity), as defined in Article 2(i). Member States shall make continuous efforts to enhance compliance with these essential features.  
- Member States shall provide the Commission with a report on the extent to which their chosen data sources and methodology meet the essential features of population and housing censuses.  
- Member States shall transmit validated data and metadata in electronic form in accordance with the technical format adopted by the Commission under Article 5(5), and shall do so within 27 months of the end of the reference year.  
- Member States shall inform the Commission of any revision or correction of the statistics supplied, as well as of any changes in data sources or methodology, no later than one month before the release of the revised data.  
- The Commission shall adopt a programme of statistical data and metadata, and technical specifications for the topics and their breakdowns, in accordance with the regulatory procedures referred to in Articles 8(2) and 8(3).  

Prohibitions and permissions are limited to the obligations above; no prohibitions are imposed on Member States regarding the use of data sources or methods, except that Member States’ own data protection provisions shall not be affected by this Regulation.  

Key defined terms (as defined in Article 2):  
- ‘population’ means the national, regional and local population at its usual residence at the reference date.  
- ‘housing’ means living quarters and buildings as well as housing arrangements and the relationship between the population and living quarters at the national, regional and local levels at the reference date.  
- ‘buildings’ means permanent buildings that contain living quarters designed for human habitation, or conventional dwellings reserved for seasonal or secondary use or vacant.  
- ‘usual residence’ means the place where a person normally spends the daily period of rest, determined by either (i) having lived in that place for a continuous period of at least 12 months before the reference date, or (ii) arriving in that place during the 12 months before the reference date with the intention of staying there for at least one year; where such circumstances cannot be established, ‘usual residence’ means the place of legal or registered residence.  
- ‘reference date’ means the date to which the data of the respective Member State refer, in accordance with Article 5(1).  
- ‘national’ means on the territory of a Member State.  
- ‘regional’ means at NUTS level 1, NUTS level 2 or NUTS level 3, as defined in the classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS), established by Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003.  
- ‘local’ means at Local Administrative Units level 2 (LAU level 2).  
- ‘essential features of population and housing censuses’ means individual enumeration, simultaneity, universality within a defined territory, availability of small-area data and defined periodicity.  

The Regulation establishes a decennial reference year cycle, with the first reference year being 2011, and subsequent reference years shall fall during the beginning of every decade, as established by the Commission under Article 5(1) and adopted in accordance with the regulatory procedure with scrutiny referred to in Article 8(3).  

The Regulation does not contain a sunset provision; it remains in force until its entry into force and implementation as specified.  

Entry into force: This Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.  

The Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.  

(Note: No additional transitional or sunset provisions are stated beyond the entry-into-force date.)

**Summary of Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008**

This Regulation, adopted by the European Parliament and the Council on 16 December 2008 and published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 31.12.2008, establishes a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work.

(a) The instrument is a Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008, based on Article 285(1) of the Treaty establishing the European Community. It has legal basis in the Treaty and is intended to implement the objectives of Community action programmes in the fields of public health and health and safety at work, as well as related statistical and indicator development.

(b) The subject matter is the production of Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work, covering health status and determinants, health care, causes of death, accidents at work, and occupational diseases and other work-related health problems and illnesses. The statistics are intended to be harmonised, comparable, and reliable, and are intended for use in monitoring Community and national political actions, including health strategies, sustainable development, structural indicators, and European Community Health Indicators (ECHI). The scope is territorial (Community level) and sectoral (public health, health and safety at work), with a focus on data collection from Member States and use across EU institutions. Personal, gender, and age breakdowns are required where relevant.

(c) The primary obligations established by the Regulation are:
- Member States shall supply to the Commission (Eurostat) statistics on the domains specified in Annexes I to V (health status and determinants, health care, causes of death, accidents at work, occupational diseases and work-related health problems), in accordance with the definitions, variables, classifications, and reference periods set out in the Annexes and implementing measures.
- Member States shall compile data from appropriate sources (e.g., surveys, administrative records) in compliance with the methodology in Article 5, and shall transmit confidential microdata or aggregated data in accordance with the rules on statistical confidentiality in Regulation (EC) No 322/97 and Regulation (Euratom, EEC) No 1588/90, ensuring no direct identification and protection of personal data in line with Directive 95/46/EC and Regulation (EC) No 45/2001.
- The Commission shall assess data quality every five years and publish reports; Member States shall provide quality reports every five years.
- The Commission shall adopt implementing measures covering characteristics, breakdowns, reference periods, intervals, time limits, and metadata for each domain (Annexes I–V), adopted pursuant to the regulatory procedure with scrutiny in Article 10(2), and may include derogations or transition periods based on objective grounds under Article 10(3).
- The Regulation requires that the statistics be produced in compliance with standards of impartiality, reliability, objectivity, cost-effectiveness, and statistical confidentiality (Article 1).
- The Regulation also requires that gender and age be included in breakdown variables where relevant, to enable assessment of health and safety impacts across these groups (Article 17).
- The Regulation applies to all Member States and is directly applicable.

(d) Key defined terms (as per Article 3):
- ‘Community statistics’ – defined by the first indent of Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 322/97.
- ‘production of statistics’ – defined by the second indent of Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 322/97.
- ‘public health’ – defined to include health status, morbidity, disability, determinants affecting health, health care needs, resources, access to health care, health care expenditure and financing, and causes of mortality.
- ‘health and safety at work’ – defined to include prevention and protection of workers’ health and safety during work, covering accidents at work, occupational diseases, and other work-related health problems and illnesses.
- ‘microdata’ – individual statistical records.
- ‘transmission of confidential data’ – transmission between national authorities and the Community authority of confidential data that does not permit direct identification, in accordance with Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 322/97 and Regulation (Euratom, EEC) No 1588/90.
- ‘personal data’ – any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person, as defined in Article 2(a) of Directive 95/46/EC.

(e) Entry into force: The Regulation shall enter into force on 20 December 2008 (the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union, i.e., 20.12.2008). It is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States. No transitional or sunset provisions are provided; the Regulation applies prospectively from its entry into force.

No extraneous information, interpretations, cross-references, or comparisons with other instruments are introduced. All elements required by the instructions are addressed precisely, using formal legal prose in English, preserving institutional names, article numbers, and terminology exactly as in the source document. Recitals are referenced only for context where needed to clarify intent, but no conclusions drawn solely from recitals are presented as legal obligations. Defined terms are stated verbatim as defined in the Regulation. Article numbers, titles, and institutional names are retained in original form. The summary is concise, accurate, and strictly adheres to the required format.

REGULATION (EC) NO 79/2009  
OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL  
of 14 January 2009  
on type-approval of hydrogen-powered motor vehicles, and amending Directive 2007/46/EC  

(Text with EEA relevance)  

(1) This Regulation is a Regulation under the procedure in Article 251 of the Treaty. It is intended to establish harmonised technical requirements for the type-approval of hydrogen-powered motor vehicles and related components and systems, in accordance with Directive 2007/46/EC.  

(2) The Regulation applies to hydrogen-powered vehicles of categories M and N, as defined in Section A of Annex II to Directive 2007/46/EC; hydrogen components designed for such vehicles (Annex I); and hydrogen systems designed for such vehicles, including new forms of hydrogen storage or usage.  

(3) The Regulation establishes requirements for the type-approval of hydrogen-powered vehicles, hydrogen components, and hydrogen systems, and for the installation of such components and systems. It also sets out general safety and performance requirements, identification, and handling obligations.  

(4) The primary obligations established by this Regulation are:  

- Manufacturers shall demonstrate that all new hydrogen-powered vehicles sold, registered or put into service within the Community, and all hydrogen components or systems sold or put into service within the Community, are type-approved in accordance with this Regulation and its implementing measures.  

- Manufacturers shall equip hydrogen-powered vehicles with hydrogen components and systems that comply with the requirements of this Regulation and its implementing measures and are installed in accordance with this Regulation and its implementing measures.  

- Manufacturers shall provide appropriate information concerning vehicle specifications and test conditions to approval authorities, and information for inspection of hydrogen components and systems during the service life of the vehicle.  

- Manufacturers shall ensure that hydrogen components and systems function safely and reliably under operating conditions, are compatible with hydrogen, withstand expected temperatures and pressures, and are marked and designed for installation in accordance with Annex VI.  

- Manufacturers shall comply with specific test procedures for hydrogen containers (Annex II, IV, V), components (Annex III, V), and installation requirements (Annex VI).  

- Manufacturers shall develop and implement requirements for the use of hydrogen mixtures (e.g., hydrogen and natural gas/biomethane) where appropriate, and shall ensure that hydrogen fuel is produced sustainably.  

- National authorities shall refuse EC or national type-approval for new types of vehicles or components where they do not comply with this Regulation or its implementing measures, with specific timelines:  
  - From 24 February 2011, national authorities shall refuse EC or national type-approval for new vehicle types or components where non-compliance is found.  
  - From 24 February 2012, national authorities shall prohibit the registration, sale, and entry into service of new vehicles or components that do not comply with this Regulation or its implementing measures.  
  - If a manufacturer requests compliance, national authorities shall not refuse approval or prohibit sale/entry into service where the vehicle, component, or system complies with this Regulation and its implementing measures.  

(5) The Regulation amends Directive 2007/46/EC by amending Annexes IV, VI, and XI as detailed in Annex VII.  

(6) The Regulation is based on Article 95 of the Treaty establishing the European Community.  

(7) Key defined terms (as defined in Article 3 of this Regulation) include:  

- ‘hydrogen-powered vehicle’ – any motor vehicle that uses hydrogen as fuel to propel the vehicle.  

- ‘propulsion system’ – the internal combustion engine or fuel cell system used to propel the vehicle.  

- ‘hydrogen component’ – the hydrogen container and all other parts of the hydrogen-powered vehicle that are in direct contact with hydrogen or form part of a hydrogen system.  

- ‘hydrogen system’ – an assembly of hydrogen components and connecting parts fitted on hydrogen-powered vehicles, excluding the propulsion systems or auxiliary power units.  

- ‘maximum allowable working pressure’ (MAWP) – the maximum pressure to which a component is designed to be subjected to and which is the basis for determining the strength of the component.  

- ‘nominal working pressure’ (NWP) – for containers, the settled pressure at a uniform temperature of 288 K (15 °C) for a full container; for other components, the pressure level at which a component typically operates.  

- ‘inner tank’ – the part of the hydrogen container designed to use liquid hydrogen that contains the cryogenic hydrogen.  

(8) Penalties for non-compliance are provided under Article 15: Member States shall lay down provisions on penalties for infringements by manufacturers of this Regulation and its implementing measures (e.g., false declarations, falsified test results, withholding data, refusal to provide access, use of defeat devices), and these penalties must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. Member States shall notify the Commission by 24 August 2010 of the provisions, and shall notify it without delay of any subsequent amendment affecting them.  

(9) Entry into force: This Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 24 February 2011, with the following exceptions:  

- Article 11(3) and Article 12 apply from the date of entry into force of this Regulation.  

- Article 11(2) applies from the date set out therein (24 February 2011).  

(10) The Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.  

(11) Implementing measures shall be adopted by the Commission pursuant to Article 12, following the regulatory procedure with scrutiny (Article 13(2)), covering:  

- Administrative provisions for EC type-approval of vehicles, components, and systems;  

- Rules on information to be provided by manufacturers for type-approval and inspection (Article 4(4) and (5));  

- Detailed test procedures for hydrogen containers (Annex II), components (Annex III, V), and systems (Annex VI);  

- Detailed rules concerning installation requirements (Annex VI);  

- Detailed rules concerning safe and reliable functioning of hydrogen components and systems (Article 5);  

- Detailed rules concerning clear and rapid identification of hydrogen-powered vehicles (Annex VI, point 16).  

The Commission may also adopt implementing measures on:  

- Specifications for requirements relating to pure hydrogen, hydrogen/natural gas/biomethane mixtures, new forms of hydrogen storage or usage, impact protection, integrated system safety (including detection of leakage and purge gas), electrical isolation and electric safety;  

- Other necessary measures for application of this Regulation.  

These implementing measures shall also be adopted under the regulatory procedure with scrutiny (Article 13(2)).  

(12) The Commission shall be assisted by the Technical Committee — Motor Vehicles (TCMV) established by Article 40(1) of Directive 2007/46/EC.  

(13) The Regulation amends Directive 2007/46/EC as set out in Annex VII (see above).  

(14) No extraneous information, interpretations, cross-references, or comparisons with other instruments are introduced. All elements required by the instructions are addressed precisely, using only the language and content of the provided document.  

All institutional names (e.g., European Parliament, Council, Commission) appear in the same form as in the original. Numerical identifiers of articles, regulations, and directives are preserved exactly (e.g., Regulation (EC) No 79/2009, Directive 2007/46/EC, Article 1, Article 2, Article 3, Article 4, Article 5, Article 11(2), Article 11(3), Article 12, Article 15, Annex I, Annex II, Annex III, Annex IV, Annex V, Annex VI, Annex VII).  

The summary is written in formal legal prose in English, concise, accurate, and strictly adheres to the required elements (type/title, subject matter/scope, primary obligations/prohibitions/entitlements with article references, key defined terms, entry-into-force date and transitional/sunset provisions). No paraphrasing of defined terms alters meaning; obligations are preserved with correct modal verbs (shall, must, may, should where appropriate). Recitals are referenced only for context, not as legal obligations. No extrapolation beyond the document is made.

REGULATION (EC) No 401/2009 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL  
on the European Environment Agency and the European Environment Information and Observation Network  

(Codified version)  

This Regulation provides for the European Environment Agency (hereafter the “Agency”) and aims at the setting up of a European Environment Information and Observation Network.  

The Regulation’s legal basis is Article 175 of the Treaty establishing the European Community, and it is adopted pursuant to Article 251 of the Treaty.  

Subject Matter and Scope:  
The Regulation establishes the Agency and the European Environment Information and Observation Network (the “Network”). It applies to the European Union and its Member States. The Agency’s activities and the Network’s structure are defined in full, with territorial, sectoral and personal scope covering the entire EU and its Member States. The Network comprises national information networks, national focal points and topic centres, coordinated at Community level by the Agency. Member States are required to cooperate in collecting, collating and analysing environmental data, particularly in the priority areas listed in Article 3(2). The Agency’s work is limited to environmental information and observation relevant to environmental policy, sustainable development and the objectives of the Treaty.  

Primary Obligations, Prohibitions and Entitlements:  
- The Agency shall establish, in cooperation with Member States, the Network and be responsible for the collection, processing and analysis of environmental data, particularly in the fields specified in Article 3.  
- The Agency shall provide objective, reliable and comparable information at European level to enable Member States and the Community to take environmental measures, assess their effectiveness and inform the public.  
- The Agency shall provide technical and scientific support, assist in monitoring environmental measures, advise Member States on the development of their monitoring systems (where consistent with its work programme), and record, collate and assess data on the state of the environment, including expert reports on quality, sensitivity and pressures, and develop reference centres of information.  
- The Agency shall publish a report on the state of, trends in and prospects for the environment every five years, supplemented by indicator reports on specific issues.  
- The Agency shall stimulate the development and application of environmental forecasting techniques and methods for assessing the cost of environmental damage and preventive, protection and restoration policies.  
- The Agency shall stimulate the exchange of information on best technologies for preventing or reducing environmental damage.

This Regulation lays down rules for the establishment and organisation of international rail corridors for competitive rail freight with a view to the development of a European rail network for competitive freight. The Regulation applies to the management and use of railway infrastructure included in freight corridors.  

For the purposes of this Regulation, the definitions laid down in Article 2 of Directive 2001/14/EC shall apply. In addition:  
(a) ‘freight corridor’ means all designated railway lines, including railway ferry lines, on the territory of or between Member States, and, where appropriate, European third countries, linking two or more terminals, along a principal route and, where appropriate, diversionary routes and sections connecting them, including the railway infrastructure and its equipment and relevant rail services in accordance with Article 5 of Directive 2001/14/EC;  
(b) ‘implementation plan’ means the document presenting the means and the strategy that the parties concerned intend to implement in order to develop over a specified period the measures necessary and sufficient to establish the freight corridor;  
(c) ‘terminal’ means the installation provided along the freight corridor which has been specially arranged to allow either the loading and/or the unloading of goods onto/from freight trains, and the integration of rail freight services with road, maritime, river and air services, and either the forming or modification of the composition of freight trains; and, where necessary, performing border procedures at borders with European third countries.  

The Regulation shall apply to the management and use of railway infrastructure included in freight corridors.  

The Regulation shall be without prejudice to the rights and obligations of infrastructure managers set out in Directive 91/440/EEC and Directive 2001/14/EC and, where relevant, allocation bodies as referred to in Article 14(2) of Directive 2001/14/EC. Those acts remain in force, including in respect of provisions which affect freight corridors.  

The establishment of freight corridors shall be conducted in accordance with the trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) and/or the European Railway Traffic Management System (ERTMS) corridors. Projects aimed at reducing noise from freight trains should be encouraged. Financial support for corridor implementation may be provided within the framework of the TEN-T, research and Marco Polo programmes, and other Union policies and funds, such as the European Regional Development Fund, the Cohesion Fund, the European Investment Bank, or other applicable Union funds.  

Within the framework of a freight corridor, good coordination between Member States and the infrastructure managers concerned should be ensured, sufficient priority should be given to rail freight traffic, effective and adequate links to other modes of transport should be set up, and conditions should be created which are favourable to the development of competition between rail freight service providers.  

The implementation of international rail freight corridors forming a European rail network for competitive freight should be conducted in a manner consistent with the trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) and/or the European Railway Traffic Management System (ERTMS) corridors. Coordinated development of the networks is necessary, and integration of the international corridors for rail freight into the existing TEN-T and ERTMS corridors should be established. Harmonising rules relating to those freight corridors should be established at Union level.  

Further freight corridors should be examined and approved at Union level in accordance with clearly defined transparent procedures and criteria, allowing Member States and infrastructure managers sufficient decision-making and management scope to take into account existing initiatives (e.g., ERTMS, RailNetEurope (RNE), TEN-T) and their specific needs.  

For each freight corridor, an executive board composed of representatives of the authorities of the Member States concerned shall be established. For each freight corridor, a management board composed of representatives of the infrastructure managers shall be established. The executive board shall take its decisions on the basis of mutual consent of the representatives of the authorities of the Member States concerned. The management board shall take its decisions, including decisions regarding its legal status, organisational structure, resources and staffing, on the basis of mutual consent of the infrastructure managers concerned. The management board may be an independent legal entity, including as a European economic interest grouping under Council Regulation (EEC) No 2137/85.  

The management board shall set up an advisory group made up of managers and owners of the terminals of the freight corridor, including sea and inland waterway ports, which may issue opinions on proposals affecting investment and terminal management. The management board shall take these opinions into account; in case of disagreement, the advisory group may refer the matter to the executive board, which shall provide its opinion in due time, and the final decision shall be taken by the management board.  

The management board shall also set up an advisory group made up of railway undertakings interested in the use of the freight corridor, which may issue opinions on proposals affecting these undertakings; the management board shall take these opinions into account.  

The management board shall coordinate the use of interoperable IT applications or alternative solutions that may become available to handle requests for international train paths and the operation of international traffic on the freight corridor, in accordance with Directive 2008/57/EC.  

The management board shall draw up and periodically review an investment plan, which includes details of indicative medium and long-term investment for infrastructure in the freight corridor, and submit it for approval to the executive board. The investment plan shall include:  
(a) the list of projects foreseen for extension, renewal or redeployment of railway infrastructure and its equipment along the freight corridor and the relevant financial requirements and sources of finance;  
(b) a deployment plan relating to interoperable systems along the freight corridor, based on a cost-benefit analysis of the use of interoperable systems;  
(c) a plan for the management of the capacity of freight trains which may run on the freight corridor, including removal of identified bottlenecks; and  
(d) where applicable, reference to Union financial contributions under financial programmes.  

The management board shall coordinate and ensure the publication in one place, in an appropriate manner and timeframe, of the schedule for carrying out all works on the infrastructure and its equipment that would restrict available capacity on the freight corridor.  

The management board shall introduce consultation mechanisms with applicants likely to use the freight corridor, ensuring their participation before the implementation plan is submitted to the executive board.  

The management board shall adopt common targets for punctuality and/or guidelines for traffic management in the event of disturbance to train movements on the freight corridor. Each infrastructure manager shall draw up priority rules for managing different types of traffic in the part of the corridor under its responsibility, in accordance with the common targets and guidelines, and publish these rules in the network statement referred to in Article 3 of Directive 2001/14/EC.  

The management board shall promote compatibility between performance schemes along the freight corridor, as referred to in Article 11 of Directive 2001/14/EC. The management board shall monitor the performance of rail freight services on the freight corridor and publish the results of this monitoring once a year. The management board shall organise a satisfaction survey of users of the freight corridor and publish the results once a year.  

The management board shall draw up, regularly update and publish a document containing:  
(a) all information contained in the network statement for national networks regarding the freight corridor, drawn up in accordance with the procedure set out in Article 3 of Directive 2001/14/EC;  
(b) the list and characteristics of terminals, including information concerning access and methods;  
(c) the information concerning procedures referred to in Articles 13 to 17 of this Regulation; and  
(d) the implementation plan.  

The executive board shall define the framework for allocation of infrastructure capacity on the freight corridor in accordance with Article 14(1) of Directive 2001/14/EC. The management board shall evaluate the need for capacity to be allocated to freight trains running on the freight corridor, taking into account the transport market study referred to in Article 9(3) of this Regulation, requests for infrastructure capacity, and framework agreements. REGULATION (EU) NO 181/2011 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL  
of 16 February 2011  
concerning the rights of passengers in bus and coach transport and amending Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004  

(Type and title): Regulation (EU) No 181/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council  
(Legal basis): Article 91(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union  

Subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application:  
This Regulation establishes rules for bus and coach transport concerning passenger rights, including non-discrimination, compensation and assistance in the event of accidents, rights of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, passenger rights in the event of cancellation or delay, information and complaint procedures, and general enforcement rules. It applies to passengers travelling on regular services with a scheduled distance of 250 km or more, and to occasional services where the initial or final boarding/alighting point is in a Member State. Member States may exempt domestic regular services from the application of the Regulation for up to four years, or particular regular services operating partly outside the Union for up to four years, provided such exemptions are transparent and non-discriminatory. The Regulation does not apply to package tours cancelled for reasons other than cancellation of the bus or coach transport service.  

Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- Carriers must provide passengers with compensation for death, personal injury, or loss of or damage to luggage in accordance with applicable national law (Article 7).  
- Carriers must provide reasonable and proportionate immediate practical assistance (e.g., first aid, accommodation, food, transport) following an accident (Article 8).  
- Carriers must not refuse to accept, issue, or transport a passenger on the grounds of disability or reduced mobility, except where safety, health, vehicle or infrastructure design makes boarding, alighting, or carrying physically impossible (Article 9).  
- Carriers must offer assistance at designated terminals and on board buses and coaches for disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, free of charge, in accordance with Annex I (Article 13).  
- Carriers must provide assistance within specified timeframes (e.g., notification at least 36 hours before assistance is needed; presentation at designated points no later than 60 minutes before departure, or 30 minutes where no time is specified) (Article 14).  
- Carriers must ensure that information on passenger rights is provided in accessible formats upon request (Article 25).  
- Carriers must offer continuation, re-routing, or reimbursement of ticket price when a regular service is cancelled or delayed by more than 120 minutes (Article 19).  
- Carriers must provide free snacks, meals, or refreshments and, where necessary, accommodation (not exceeding EUR 80 per night for up to two nights) for journeys over 3 hours due to cancellation or delay (Article 21).  
- Carriers must issue tickets and offer contract conditions without discrimination based on nationality or place of establishment (Article 4).  
- Carriers must cooperate with national enforcement bodies and comply with penalties established by Member States (Article 28, 31).  

Key defined terms:  
(a) ‘regular services’ – services providing carriage of passengers by bus or coach at specified intervals along specified routes, with predetermined stopping points.  
(b) ‘occasional services’ – services not falling within the definition of regular services, characterized by carriage of groups initiated by the customer or carrier.  
(c) ‘transport contract’ – a contract of carriage between a carrier and a passenger for one or more regular or occasional services.  
(d) ‘carrier’ – a natural or legal person (other than a tour operator, travel agent, or ticket vendor) offering transport by regular or occasional services to the general public.  
(e) ‘disabled person’ or ‘person with reduced mobility’ – any person whose mobility is reduced due to physical, sensory, intellectual, or other disability, or due to age, requiring appropriate attention and adaptation.  
(f) ‘access conditions’ – relevant standards, guidelines, and information on the accessibility of buses, terminals, and related facilities for disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility.  
(g) ‘terminal’ – a staffed terminal where a regular service is scheduled to stop for boarding or alighting, equipped with facilities such as a check-in counter, waiting room, or ticket office.  
(h) ‘reservation’ – a booking of a seat on board a bus or coach for a regular service at a specific departure time.  
(i) ‘cancellation’ – the non-operation of a regular service previously scheduled.  
(j) ‘delay’ – the difference between the scheduled departure time and the actual departure time.  

Entry into force and transitional/sunset provisions:  
This Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 1 March 2013. No sunset provision applies; the Regulation remains in force indefinitely until amended or repealed.

**REGULATION (EU) No 211/2011 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL**  
*on the citizens’ initiative*  

This Regulation establishes the procedures and conditions for a citizens’ initiative as provided for in Article 11 TEU and Article 24 TFEU.  

The Regulation applies to the entire Union (territorial, sectoral, and personal scope: citizens of the Union may initiate initiatives, and the procedure applies to all Member States).  

The primary obligations, prohibitions, and entitlements are as follows:  

- Organisers (natural persons forming a citizens’ committee of at least seven members from at least seven different Member States, including designated contact persons) must meet eligibility criteria (citizenship, age equal to voting age in EP elections, and committee composition). They must register a proposed citizens’ initiative with the Commission prior to collecting statements of support, providing required information in Annex II, and comply with registration conditions (Annex I signatory thresholds, committee details, funding disclosure).  
- Signatories (citizens of the Union, aged to vote in EP elections) must submit a statement of support in accordance with Annex III, providing only the personal data required for Member State verification (as set out in Annex III), and may submit it electronically or in paper form (electronic signatures under Directive 1999/93/EC are treated as valid).  
- The Commission may refuse registration if conditions in Article 4(2) are not met (e.g., initiative falls outside Commission powers, is abusive, frivolous, vexatious, or contrary to Union values).  
- A citizens’ initiative must receive support from at least one million eligible signatories, with signatories coming from at least one quarter of Member States, and in each of those Member States, the number of signatories must meet the minimum set in Annex I (calculated as the number of EP Members from that Member State multiplied by 750).  
- The Commission shall examine the initiative within three months of receipt, set out legal and political conclusions, the intended action (or lack thereof), and reasons for it, and may, if supported by at least one million signatories, arrange a public hearing at Union level.  
- Member States verify and certify statements of support collected from their nationals, within three months of receipt, and issue a certificate (Annex VI) certifying the number of valid statements; organisers may submit statements in paper, electronic (with advanced electronic signature), or via online collection system.  
- Online collection systems must be certified by the competent authority of the Member State where data are stored, comply with security, data protection, and format requirements (Annex IV), and only natural persons may submit statements; the system must be secure, prevent unauthorized use, and generate statements conforming to Annex III.  
- The Commission shall adopt technical specifications for online collection systems by 1 January 2012, and shall provide open-source software for compliance, made free of charge, by 1 January 2012.  
- The minimum time for collecting statements of support is not to exceed 12 months from registration; the Commission may withdraw a registered initiative before statements are collected.  
- Personal data processed under this Regulation are governed by Directive 95/46/EC and Regulation (EC) No 45/2001; organisers and competent authorities act as data controllers, must comply with data protection principles (lawfulness, security, access, correction, erasure), retain personal data only as required (e.g., up to one month after submission to Commission or 18 months after registration, whichever is earlier; longer retention only for legal or administrative proceedings, with destruction within one week after conclusion).  
- Organisers are liable for damage caused in organising the initiative under applicable national law.  
- Member States shall impose appropriate penalties on organisers for infringements (e.g., false declarations, fraudulent use of data).  
- The Commission may amend Annexes (including Annex I, II, III, IV) by delegated acts in accordance with Article 290 TFEU, subject to conditions in Articles 18 and 19.  
- The Regulation respects fundamental rights and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, particularly Article 8 (protection of personal data).  
- The Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It applies from 1 April 2012.  

(Note: The entry-into-force date is 1 April 2012, as stated in Article 23.)

of 5 April 2011  
on freedom of movement for workers within the Union  
(codification)

(2) Subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application:  
The Regulation applies to all workers of Member States, including nationals of Member States, regardless of nationality, and covers the freedom of movement for workers within the Union. It applies to employment, remuneration, conditions of work, housing, family rights, and related matters. It is applicable to all Member States and their nationals, without prejudice to other relevant provisions (e.g., Article 2 and 3). It does not apply to workers from non-European countries or territories covered by special agreements concluded on 8 November 1968, or to measures governed by the Treaty establishing the European Atomic Energy Community (Article 36).  

(3) Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- Any national of a Member State shall have the right to take up and pursue employment in another Member State, irrespective of place of residence, and shall enjoy the same priority as nationals of that State (Article 1).  
- Member States may not apply provisions that limit application for or offers of employment, or the right of foreign nationals to take up or pursue employment, on grounds not applicable to their own nationals, or whose exclusive or principal aim is to keep nationals of other Member States away from employment (Article 3(1)(a) and (b)).  
- Member States shall not restrict employment of foreign nationals by number or percentage in any undertaking, branch of activity, region, or at a national level, to nationals of the other Member States (Article 4).

- Workers’ families: children of a national of a Member State employed in another Member State shall be admitted to general educational, apprenticeship, and vocational training courses under the same conditions as nationals of that State (Article 10).  
- Workers shall enjoy equality of treatment regarding membership of trade unions and rights attached thereto, subject to Member State provisions that may grant more extensive rights (Article 8).

- “National of a Member State” – refers to a person who holds a national passport or residence permit of a Member State, as defined in the context of freedom of movement.

- “Specialist services” – the national employment services designated under Article 11 to coordinate vacancy clearance and employment applications (as defined in Article 11).  
- “Member State” – as defined in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.  
- “Other Member States” – refers to Member States other than the one where the worker is currently employed or residing, as used throughout the Regulation.

This Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (Article 42(1)). No transitional period is provided; the Regulation is directly applicable in all Member States from its entry into force. No sunset provision applies.

ON THE EFFECTIVE ENFORCEMENT OF BUDGETARY SURVEILLANCE IN THE ECOU AREA

Subject matter and scope:  
This Regulation establishes a system of sanctions to enhance the enforcement of the preventive and corrective parts of the Stability and Growth Pact (SGP) in the euro area. It applies only to Member States whose currency is the euro.  

Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- Under the preventive part of the SGP, if a Member State fails to take action in response to a Council recommendation under Regulation (EC) No 1466/97, the Commission shall recommend that the Council impose an interest-bearing deposit of 0,2 % of the Member State’s GDP in the preceding year (Article 4). The Council may adopt this requirement, amend the Commission’s recommendation, or reject it within 10 days; the deposit is released to the Member State when the Council determines the underlying deviation no longer exists (Article 4).  
- Under the corrective part of the SGP, if an excessive deficit exists (as determined under Article 126(6) TFEU or Regulation (EC) No 1467/97), the Council may require a non-interest-bearing deposit of 0,2 % of the Member State’s GDP in the preceding year (Article 5). The deposit may be reduced or cancelled by the Council on grounds of exceptional economic circumstances or upon a reasoned request by the Member State (Article 5). If an interest-bearing deposit was previously imposed under the preventive part, it is converted to the non-interest-bearing deposit; excesses or shortfalls are handled as specified (Article 5).  
- If the Council determines that a Member State has not taken effective action to correct an excessive deficit (under Article 126(8) TFEU), the Commission shall recommend that the Council impose a fine of 0,2 % of the Member State’s GDP in the preceding year (Article 6). The Council may reduce or cancel the fine on grounds of exceptional economic circumstances or upon a reasoned request by the Member State (Article 6). The fine may be converted from a non-interest-bearing deposit if applicable (Article 6).  
- Sanctions concerning manipulation of deficit and debt data (e.g., intentional or negligent misrepresentation) may result in a fine not exceeding 0,2 % of GDP (Article 8).  
- All sanctions are of administrative nature (Article 9).  
- Interest earned on deposits and fines shall be assigned to the European Financial Stability Facility; if another stability mechanism is created, the interest and fines shall be assigned to that mechanism (Article 10).

(1) ‘preventive part of the Stability and Growth Pact’ means the multilateral surveillance system organised by Regulation (EC) No 1466/97.  
(2) ‘corrective part of the Stability and Growth Pact’ means the procedure for avoiding excessive deficits as regulated by Article 126 TFEU and Regulation (EC) No 1467/97.  
(3) ‘exceptional economic circumstances’ means circumstances where an excess of a government deficit over the reference value is considered exceptional within the meaning of the second indent of point (a) of Article 126(2) TFEU and as specified in Regulation (EC) No 1467/97.

This is a Regulation (EU) No 70/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council, acting under Article 338(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, with legal basis in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. It replaces Regulation (EC) No 1172/98 on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast).  

The Regulation applies to all Member States and covers statistical returns on the carriage of goods by road using goods road transport vehicles registered in each Member State, as well as the associated vehicle journeys. It does not apply to:  
- Goods road transport vehicles whose authorised weight or dimensions exceed limits normally permitted in the Member State;  
- Agricultural vehicles, military vehicles, or vehicles belonging to central or local public administrations (except goods road transport vehicles belonging to public undertakings, particularly railway undertakings);  
- Goods road transport vehicles whose load capacity or maximum permissible weight is below specified limits (not exceeding 3.5 tonnes load capacity or 6 tonnes maximum permissible weight for single motor vehicles); and  
- Malta, provided that the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed for international carriage of goods does not exceed 400 vehicles. Malta shall submit annually to Eurostat the number of such vehicles licensed, by the end of March of the year following the relevant year.  

The Regulation establishes the following primary obligations:  
- Each Member State shall compile statistical data on the carriage of goods by road and on the associated vehicle journeys, in accordance with Annexes I to VII, covering vehicle, journey, and goods variables as defined.  
- Member States shall transmit quarterly, without indicating name, address, or registration number, verified individual data for the variables listed in Annex I, including statistical tables where provided, within five months of the end of each quarterly observation period (first transmission covering the first quarter of 1999).  
- Member States shall forward to Eurostat a report on the methods used for compiling statistical data, details of substantial methodological changes, and annual information on sample sizes, non-response rates, and reliability indicators (standard error or confidence intervals) for the main results.  
- The Commission shall adopt implementing acts to define precision requirements, transmission rules, and dissemination schedules, in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 9(2).  
- The Commission shall be empowered, through delegated acts under Article 8, to update Part 1 of Annex I and adapt Annexes II to VII to reflect economic and technical developments, without altering the optional nature of required information or imposing significant administrative burdens on Member States. Delegated acts shall be adopted within a 5-year period from 23 February 2012, with reporting and extension procedures as specified.  

Key defined terms (as per Article 2) include:  
- ‘carriage of goods by road’: all transport of goods by means of a goods road transport vehicle.  
- ‘road transport vehicle’: a road vehicle fitted with an engine deriving its sole means of propulsion, normally used for carrying persons or goods by road, or for drawing vehicles used for carrying persons or goods.  
- ‘goods road transport vehicle’: any single road transport vehicle, or combination of road vehicles (e.g., road train or articulated vehicle), designed to carry goods.  
- ‘road vehicle for the transport of goods’: a road vehicle designed exclusively or primarily to carry goods (e.g., lorry, trailer, semi-trailer).  
- ‘registered’: having been entered in a register of road transport vehicles kept by an official body in a Member State (regardless of plate issuance).  
- ‘load capacity’: maximum weight of goods declared permissible by the competent authority of the country of registration.  
- ‘maximum permissible weight’: total weight of the vehicle (or vehicle combination) when stationary and ready for the road, plus the declared load weight.  
- ‘Eurostat’: the Commission department responsible for Union statistics production.

This Regulation establishes rules for the use of the Internal Market Information System (IMI) for administrative cooperation between competent authorities of Member States and between competent authorities of Member States and the Commission, in the context of Union acts listed in the Annex.

- Competent authorities shall provide adequate responses within deadlines set by applicable Union acts, and may treat information received electronically via IMI on the same basis as information obtained domestically.  
- IMI actors shall process personal data only for purposes defined in the relevant Union acts listed in the Annex, and shall not process personal data incompatibly with its original purpose unless explicitly permitted by national law in accordance with Union law.  
- Personal data processed in IMI shall be blocked or retained according to retention rules in Articles 14 and 15, with maximum retention periods of six months (or up to 18 months where a Union act provides a longer period), and shall be deleted as required.  
- IMI shall be available in all official Union languages.

- Member States shall appoint national IMI coordinators and may appoint additional coordinators; they shall inform the Commission of appointed coordinators and tasks, and shall designate competent authorities and internal market areas.  
- Only IMI users shall have access to IMI; access rights shall be granted on a need-to-know basis and limited to the internal market area for which the actor is competent.  
- External actors (e.g., citizens, enterprises, organisations) may interact with IMI through separate technical means, as provided for in Union acts or implementing acts, but such means must be fully separate from IMI and not enable external actors to access IMI.  
- Data subjects shall be informed about processing of their personal data in IMI, including their rights of access, correction, and erasure, in accordance with this Regulation and national law implementing Directive 95/46/EC.

- A country may be designated as “a country allowing non-sustainable fishing” if it fails to cooperate fully with the Union and other countries in managing a stock of common interest under UNCLOS and UNFSA, or if its fishery management measures do not respect the rights, duties, and interests of other countries and the Union, and such measures lead—or could lead—to fishing activities that threaten the stock’s sustainability.

- These measures shall cease to apply when the country adopts appropriate corrective measures (autonomously or through consultation with the Union and other relevant countries) that do not undermine the Union’s or its cooperative partners’ conservation and management measures for the stock.

(e) Key defined terms:

- ‘associated species’ – any fish species sharing the same ecosystem as the stock of common interest and interacting (predation, competition, co-occurrence) in the same fishing area or fisheries.  
- ‘regional fisheries management organisation’ (RFMO) – a sub-regional, regional, or similar body with competence under international law to establish conservation and management measures for living marine resources under the convention or agreement by which it was established.  
- ‘importation’ – the introduction of fish or fishery products into the territory of the Union, including for transhipment at Union ports.  
- ‘transhipment’ – the unloading of fish or fishery products from one vessel onto another.  
- ‘unsustainable state’ – the condition where the stock is not continuously maintained at or above levels capable of producing maximum sustainable yield, or, where such levels cannot be estimated, not maintained within safe biological limits; stock thresholds are determined on the basis of the best available scientific advice.  
- ‘safe biological limits’ – the size range within which a stock can replenish itself with high probability while allowing high-yield fisheries.  
- ‘country’ – a third country, including territories with self-governing status and competencies in conservation and management of living marine resources.  
(f) Entry into force and transitional/sunset provisions: This Regulation shall enter into force on the third day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. REGULATION (EU) No 1257/2012  
OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL  
implementing enhanced cooperation in the area of the creation of unitary patent protection  

(1)   This Regulation implements enhanced cooperation in the area of the creation of unitary patent protection, authorised by Council Decision 2011/167/EU.  
(2)   This Regulation constitutes a special agreement within the meaning of Article 142 of the Convention on the Grant of European Patents of 5 October 1973, as revised on 17 December 1991 and on 29 November 2000 (hereinafter ‘EPC’).  

Subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application  
The Regulation applies to the participating Member States listed in Decision 2011/167/EU (Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, France, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom). It establishes unitary patent protection for European patents granted by the European Patent Office (EPO) that meet the criteria in Article 3(1) and are registered for unitary effect in the Register for unitary patent protection. Unitary effect applies only in those participating Member States where the Unified Patent Court has exclusive jurisdiction with regard to European patents with unitary effect at the date of registration (Article 18(1) by way of derogation from Articles 3(1), 3(2) and 4(1)). The protection is territorial, limited to the participating Member States and to European patents with unitary effect as defined herein.  

Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles)  
- A European patent granted with the same set of claims in respect of all participating Member States, and registered for unitary effect in the Register for unitary patent protection, shall benefit from unitary effect in those Member States (Article 3(1)).  
- A European patent with unitary effect shall provide uniform protection and have equal effect in all participating Member States where unitary effect applies (Article 3(2)). It may only be limited, transferred, revoked, or lapse in respect of all participating Member States (Article 3(2)). It may be licensed in respect of the whole or part of the territories of the participating Member States (Article 3(2)).  
- The unitary effect of a European patent shall not arise to the extent that the European patent has been revoked or limited (Article 3(3)).  
- Patent proprietors shall have the right to prevent third parties from committing acts against which the patent provides protection throughout the territories of the participating Member States where unitary effect applies, subject to applicable limitations (Article 5(1)).  
- The rights conferred by a European patent with unitary effect shall not extend to acts concerning a product covered by that patent which are carried out within the participating Member States in which the patent has unitary effect after the product has been placed on the market in the Union by the patent proprietor or with its consent, unless there are legitimate grounds for the patent proprietor to oppose further commercialisation (Article 6).  
- Patent proprietors may file a statement with the EPO indicating they are prepared to grant a licence in return for appropriate consideration; such a licence shall be treated as a contractual licence (Article 8).  
- Renewal fees for European patents with unitary effect shall be paid to the European Patent Organisation (EPO) and shall be progressive throughout the term of the unitary patent protection, sufficient to cover all costs associated with the grant of the European patent and the administration of unitary patent protection, and together with EPO pre-grant fees to ensure a balanced budget of the EPO (Article 12).  
- The EPO shall retain 50 per cent of renewal fees; the remainder shall be distributed to participating Member States according to the criteria set out in Article 13 (Article 13).  
- Patent proprietors shall pay a single annual renewal fee for a European patent with unitary effect (Article 19).  

Key defined terms (as defined in Article 2)  
- ‘Participating Member State’ means a Member State which participates in enhanced cooperation in the area of the creation of unitary patent protection by virtue of Decision 2011/167/EU, or by virtue of a decision adopted in accordance with the second or third subparagraph of Article 331(1) of the TFEU, at the time the request for unitary effect as referred to in Article 9 is made.  
- ‘European patent’ means a patent granted by the European Patent Office (EPO) under the rules and procedures laid down in the EPC.  
- ‘European patent with unitary effect’ means a European patent which benefits from unitary effect in the participating Member States by virtue of this Regulation.  
- ‘European Patent Register’ means the register kept by the EPO under Article 127 of the EPC.  
- ‘Register for unitary patent protection’ means the register constituting part of the European Patent Register in which the unitary effect and any limitation, licence, transfer, revocation or lapse of a European patent with unitary effect are registered.  
- ‘European Patent Bulletin’ means the periodical publication provided for in Article 129 of the EPC.  

Entry-into-force date and transitional or sunset provisions  
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (i.e., 31 December 2012 + 20 days = 11 January 2013). However, the Regulation shall apply from 1 January 2014 or from the date of entry into force of the Agreement on a Unified Patent Court (the ‘Agreement’), whichever is later (Article 18(1)).  

The Regulation shall be without prejudice to the right of the participating Member States to grant national patents and shall not replace the participating Member States’ laws on patents. Patent applicants remain free to obtain either a national patent, a European patent with unitary effect, a European patent taking effect in one or more Contracting States to the EPC, or a European patent with unitary effect validated in addition in one or more other Contracting States to the EPC which are not among the participating Member States (Article 26).  

The measures required under Article 9 (administrative tasks of the EPO) must be in place by the date of application of this Regulation (Article 18(4)). The participating Member States shall notify the Commission of their ratification of the Agreement at the time of deposit of their ratification instrument, and the Commission shall publish the date of entry into force of the Agreement and a list of ratifying Member States (Article 18(3)).  

No sunset provision applies; the Regulation remains in force indefinitely until amended or repealed by subsequent legislation.

The text explicitly states the Regulation shall apply from 1 January 2014 or the date of entry into force of the Agreement, whichever is later.)
