COUNCIL REGULATION (EU, EURATOM) No 1311/2013  
of 2 December 2013  

Type and title: Regulation (EU, EURATOM) – Multiannual Financial Framework for the years 2014 to 2020  

Legal basis: Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Article 312; Treaty establishing the European Atomic Energy Community, Article 106a  

Subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application:  
The Regulation establishes a multiannual financial framework (MFF) applicable to the European Union for the financial years 2014 to 2020. It applies to all Member States and covers all budgetary appropriations under the general budget of the Union, including commitment and payment appropriations, cohesion policy, and special instruments. The framework is territorial in scope (EU-28 at the time of adoption) and sectoral, covering all budgetary domains defined in the MFF (e.g., Smart and Inclusive Growth, Sustainable Growth, Security and Citizenship, Global Europe, Administration, Compensations), as well as cohesion policy and special financing mechanisms. It does not apply to non-EU entities or external actors.  

Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- The European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission shall comply with the annual expenditure ceilings set out in the MFF for commitment and payment appropriations (Article 3(1)).  
- The MFF ceilings for commitment and payment appropriations must be respected; where special instruments (e.g., Emergency Aid Reserve, Flexibility Instrument, Contingency Margin, Global margin for commitments, etc.) are used to finance expenditure exceeding MFF ceilings, the commitment appropriations may be entered in the budget above the relevant MFF ceilings where necessary (Article 3(2)).  
- The total payments required for each year must not produce a call-in rate for own resources exceeding the own-resources ceiling set in Council Decision 2007/436/EC, Euratom (Article 4).  
- The Commission shall adjust the MFF ceilings annually via technical adjustments (Article 6), including revaluation at year-end prices, calculation of margins under the own-resources ceiling, Contingency Margin, global payment and commitment margins (Article 6(1)).  
- The Commission shall review and adjust cohesion policy envelopes in 2016, based on forecasts and crisis conditions, ensuring adjustments do not exceed EUR 4 billion net effect (Article 7).  
- The MFF may be revised in cases of unforeseen circumstances (Article 17), or in relation to enlargement, reunification of Cyprus, revision of Treaties, or new rules/programmes for structural funds (Articles 19–22), or due to implementation issues (Article 18).  
- Special instruments (e.g., Emergency Aid Reserve, Flexibility Instrument, Global margin for commitments, youth employment flexibility) provide mechanisms for financing specific expenditures outside MFF ceilings, subject to defined limits and procedures (Articles 9–15).  
- The Commission shall present a proposal for a new MFF before 1 January 2018 (Article 14). If no new framework is adopted before 31 December 2020, the MFF ceilings and provisions of the last year shall remain in force until a new regulation is adopted (Article 25).

Subject matter and scope:  
This Regulation establishes rules and procedures for the introduction of noise-related operating restrictions at Union airports, applying the Balanced Approach. It applies only to Member States where an airport with more than 50,000 civil aircraft movements per calendar year is located and where the introduction of noise-related operating restrictions is being considered at such an airport. - Member States must designate competent authorities responsible for adopting operating restrictions, which must be independent of any organisation involved in airport operation, air transport, or air navigation service provision, or representing the interests thereof, and of residents near the airport (Article 3).  
- Competent authorities must assess noise situations regularly in accordance with Directive 2002/49/EC and must follow the Balanced Approach methodology when determining whether operating restrictions are needed (Article 5, Article 6).  
- Operating restrictions may only be introduced when other Balanced Approach measures (reduction at source, land-use planning, noise abatement procedures) are insufficient to achieve the noise abatement objective (Article 5(3), Article 8).  
- Operating restrictions must be introduced only when other measures are not sufficient; they must not be applied as a first resort unless justified under the Balanced Approach (Article 5(3), Article 8).  
- The Regulation prohibits imposing noise quality objectives that override those in Directive 2002/49/EC or other Union rules; it does not set new noise quality objectives (Article 9, Article 10, Article 19).  
- Member States may exempt marginally compliant aircraft from operating restrictions in developing countries, provided the aircraft meet certification standards, were operated in the Union within the five-year period preceding entry into force, were registered in that country, and continue to be operated there (Article 9).  
- Exceptional operations (e.g., humanitarian flights, maintenance) may be exempted from operating restrictions on a case-by-case basis (Article 10).  
- The Regulation does not require review or amendment of existing operating restrictions already in force before 13 June 2016 (Article 14).  
- The Commission may notify competent authorities if a process for introducing operating restrictions does not comply with this Regulation; the competent authority must examine the notification and inform the Commission before implementing the restriction (Article 8).

- ‘aircraft’ means fixed-wing aircraft with a maximum certificated take-off mass of 34,000 kg or more, or with a certificated maximum internal accommodation of 19 passenger seats or more (excluding crew-only seats).  
- ‘airport’ means an airport with more than 50,000 civil aircraft movements per calendar year, based on the average of the last three calendar years.  
- ‘Balanced Approach’ means the ICAO process that considers reduction at source, land-use planning and management, noise abatement operational procedures, and operating restrictions in a consistent, cost-effective manner on an airport-by-airport basis.  
- ‘marginally compliant aircraft’ means aircraft certified under the Chicago Convention limits with a cumulative margin of less than 8 EPNdB during a transitional period ending 14 June 2020, or less than 10 EPNdB after that date (as defined in Article 2(4)).

DIRECTIVE (EU) 2017/1371 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL

(1) Type and title: Directive  
(2) Legal basis in the Treaties: Article 83(2) TFEU  
(3) Subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application:  
The Directive establishes minimum rules concerning the definition of criminal offences and sanctions for fraud and other illegal activities affecting the Union’s financial interests. It applies to all Member States, including those not bound by the Convention on the protection of the European Communities’ financial interests (replaced by this Directive). The scope covers fraud affecting Union financial interests, including revenues, expenditure, assets, and financial operations (e.g., borrowing and lending), as well as serious VAT fraud involving cross-border schemes. It applies to criminal offences committed by individuals, legal persons, and public officials, and to conduct involving Union funds, regardless of where it occurs or who is involved. The Directive does not apply to disciplinary or non-criminal measures, and it does not affect the application of administrative Union measures under Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 2988/95.  

(4) Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- Member States shall establish that fraud affecting Union financial interests constitutes a criminal offence when committed intentionally (Article 3(1)).  
- Member States shall adopt national law so that specific acts or omissions listed in Article 3 (e.g., false statements, misapplication of funds, non-disclosure) constitute criminal offences (Article 3(2)).  
- Member States shall ensure that legal persons can be held liable for criminal offences committed for their benefit (Article 6).  
- Member States shall impose criminal sanctions on natural persons for offences involving considerable damage or advantage (Article 7), including a maximum penalty of at least four years’ imprisonment where damage exceeds EUR 100,000 or is otherwise deemed considerable (Article 7(3)).  
- Member States shall ensure that offences against the common VAT system are treated as serious where they involve cross-border schemes, territorial spread across two or more Member States, and total damage of at least EUR 10,000,000 (Article 2(2), Article 3(d)).  
- Member States shall provide for jurisdiction over offences committed within their territory or by their nationals, or by officials under the Staff Regulations (Article 11).  
- Member States shall establish limitation periods of at least five years for offences punishable by a maximum penalty of at least four years’ imprisonment (Article 12).  
- Member States shall cooperate with the Commission, Eurojust, and other Union bodies on cross-border investigations and provide technical/operational assistance (Article 15).  
- The Directive does not create obligations to apply criminal penalties or other enforcement mechanisms; Member States may retain or apply administrative measures in parallel (Article 31).  

(5) Key defined terms (as defined in Article 2):  
- ‘Union’s financial interests’ means all revenues, expenditure, and assets covered by, acquired through, or due to the Union budget; budgets of Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies; and funds directly or indirectly managed or monitored by them.  
- ‘legal person’ means an entity having legal personality under applicable law, except for States, public bodies exercising State authority, or public international organisations.  
- ‘public official’ means a Union official, national official (including officials of other Member States or third countries, and persons holding executive, administrative, judicial, or other public service functions involving management of Union funds), and any other person assigned and exercising a public service function concerning Union financial interests (as defined in Article 4(4)).  
- ‘misappropriation’ is defined as the action of a public official who, entrusted with management of funds or assets, commits or disposes of them contrary to their intended purpose, damaging Union financial interests.

The Directive shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (Article 19). This Directive (EU) 2018/958 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on 28 June 2018, is a Directive. Its legal basis is the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, specifically Article 46, Article 53(1) and Article 62 TFEU.

The subject matter of the Directive is the establishment of a proportionality test to be applied by Member States before adopting new, or amending existing, legislative, regulatory or administrative provisions that restrict access to, or the pursuit of, regulated professions, in order to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market and to prevent disproportionate measures that may hinder the exercise of fundamental rights, including freedom of establishment, freedom to provide services, and freedom to choose an occupation.

The Directive applies to all Member States and concerns legislative, regulatory or administrative provisions restricting access to, or the pursuit of, regulated professions that fall within the scope of Directive 2005/36/EC. It applies to new or amended provisions, including those regulating access to professional activities, use of professional titles, reserved activities, and other forms of regulation of professions. It does not apply where specific requirements concerning the regulation of a given profession are established in a separate Union act that does not leave Member States a choice in how to transpose them. The Directive is without prejudice to Member States’ competence to define the organisation and content of education and training systems, and to exclude provisions that do not restrict access or pursuit of professions (e.g., editorial amendments, technical adaptations, modernisation of training regulations).

The primary obligations established by the Directive are:

- Member States must conduct a proportionality assessment before introducing or amending any new or existing provisions restricting access to, or the pursuit of, regulated professions. The assessment must be proportionate to the nature, content and impact of the provision.
- The burden of proof of justification and proportionality lies with the Member State, which must provide a detailed, objective and independent analysis demonstrating genuine risks to public interest objectives and that the measure is suitable, appropriate and not excessive in achieving those objectives.
- Member States must ensure that any restriction is justified by public interest objectives, including those recognized in case law (e.g., public health, public security, public safety, consumer protection, social security equilibrium, environmental protection, animal health, cultural policy, etc.), and that purely economic or purely administrative reasons are not sufficient.
- The measure must be suitable for securing the attainment of the objective pursued and must not go beyond what is necessary (i.e., must be proportionate). This includes considering whether less restrictive means could achieve the same objective, especially where consumer protection is the sole justification and risks are limited to professional–consumer relationships.
- Member States must assess the impact of the measure on free movement of persons and services, consumer choice, and quality of service, and ensure the restriction is proportionate to the importance of the objectives pursued and the expected gains.
- Member States must consider a range of criteria relevant to the regulated profession, including the connection between professional activities and required qualifications, complexity of tasks, alternative routes to qualification, sharing of activities, degree of autonomy, scientific and technological developments, and the effect of combined restrictions.
- For healthcare professions, the Directive requires additional consideration of human health protection, accessibility, quality, safety, and patient safety, in line with the Charter and TFEU.
- Member States must provide information and involve stakeholders (citizens, service recipients, professional associations, social partners) before adopting new or amended provisions, and may conduct public consultations where appropriate.

This Regulation establishes common rules for the production of rail transport statistics at Union level. It applies to all railways in the Union. Reporting thresholds apply: undertakings meeting volume criteria (≥200 000 000 tonne‑km goods or ≥100 000 000 passenger‑km passengers) must report under Annexes I/II; others report aggregated data under Annex VIII. (2) Legal basis: Article 338(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

(4) Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- Member States shall calculate GNI in accordance with Article 1 and the definitions in Annex A to Regulation (EU) No 549/2013 (ESA 2010). (Article 1, Article 2)  
- Member States shall provide the Commission (Eurostat) with GNI aggregates and components, together with a quality report detailing methodology, changes, and revisions, before 1 October each year for the preceding year. (Article 2)  
- Member States shall provide an inventory of sources and methods for producing GNI data and components, consistent with ESA 2010, in accordance with Annex A to Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. (Article 3)  
- The Commission shall verify the sources, methods, and compliance with ESA 2010 via a verification model based on peer review and cost-effectiveness, and shall adopt delegated acts to define the list of issues to be addressed in each verification cycle, ensuring reliability, exhaustiveness, and comparability. - The Commission shall adopt delegated acts for a period of five years from 18 April 2019, subject to periodic review and possible extension, and may revoke them at any time by the European Parliament or Council. (Article 7)  
- The Commission shall carry out GNI information visits in Member States, respecting statistical confidentiality rules, and may invite national accounts experts from other Member States (voluntary participation). (Article 6)  
- The Commission shall establish an expert group to advise on comparability, reliability, and exhaustiveness of GNI calculations and issue annual opinions. (Article 4)

(5) Key defined terms (as used in the Regulation, preserved verbatim):

- “Gross domestic product at market prices (GDP)” – defined in Article 1(2) per ESA 2010 (three approaches: production, expenditure, income).  
- “ESA 2010” – the European System of Accounts 2010, established by Regulation (EU) No 549/2013.  
- “GNI aggregates and their components” – the total and component figures of GNI as defined in Article 1, to be transmitted by Member States.  
- “Quality report” – the report accompanying GNI data transmission (Article 2) detailing methodology, significant changes, and revisions.  
- “Inventory of the sources and methods used to produce GNI data and their components” – the structured description of data production methods, consistent with ESA 2010 (Article 3).  
- “Verification model” – the Commission’s model used to verify GNI data quality, reliability, exhaustiveness, and ESA 2010 compliance (Article 5).  
- “GNI information visits” – visits by the Commission (Eurostat) to Member States to verify GNI quality and compliance (Article 6).  
- “Statistical confidentiality” – rules set out in Chapter V of Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 (Article 6(2)).

This Regulation establishes uniform rules on the publication of national provisions concerning marketing requirements for collective investment undertakings and on marketing communications addressed to investors, as well as common principles concerning fees and charges levied on managers of collective investment undertakings in relation to their cross-border activities. The Regulation shall apply to:  
(a) alternative investment fund managers;  
(b) UCITS management companies, including any UCITS which has not designated a UCITS management company;  
(c) EuVECA managers; and  
(d) EuSEF managers.  

Definitions (Article 3):  
(a) ‘alternative investment funds’ or ‘AIFs’ means AIFs as defined in point (a) of Article 4(1) of Directive 2011/61/EU, and include EuVECA, EuSEF and ELTIF;  
(b) ‘alternative investment fund managers’ or ‘AIFMs’ means AIFMs as defined in point (b) of Article 4(1) of Directive 2011/61/EU and authorised in accordance with Article 6 of that Directive;  
(c) ‘EuVECA manager’ means a manager of a qualifying venture capital fund as defined in point (c) of the first paragraph of Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 345/2013 and registered in accordance with Article 14 of that Regulation;  
(d) ‘EuSEF manager’ means a manager of a qualifying social entrepreneurship fund as defined in point (c) of Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) No 346/2013 and registered in accordance with Article 15 of that Regulation;  
(e) ‘competent authorities’ means competent authorities as defined in point (h) of Article 2(1) of Directive 2009/65/EC or in point (f) of Article 4(1) of Directive 2011/61/EU or competent authorities of the EU AIF as defined in point (h) of Article 4(1) of Directive 2011/61/EU;  
(f) ‘home Member State’ means the Member State in which the AIFM, the EuVECA manager, the EuSEF manager or the UCITS management company has its registered office;  
(g) ‘UCITS’ means a UCITS authorised in accordance with Article 5 of Directive 2009/65/EC;  
(h) ‘UCITS management company’ means a management company as defined in point (b) of Article 2(1) of Directive 2009/65/EC.  

The Regulation is based on the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Article 114 TFUE.  

Scope and application:  
The Regulation applies to the subject matter and territorial, sectoral, and personal scope as defined in Article 2, covering alternative investment fund managers, UCITS management companies, EuVECA managers, and EuSEF managers. It is intended to facilitate cross-border distribution of collective investment undertakings (AIFs, UCITS, EuVECA, EuSEF) and to ensure uniform marketing communications and fee structures across Member States.

- UCITS management companies shall ensure that marketing communications do not contradict or diminish the significance of prospectus or key investor information required by Directive 2009/65/EC (Article 4, paragraph 2), and shall specify where, how, and in which language investors can obtain prospectus, key investor information, and provide hyperlinks (Article 4, paragraph 2).

- Marketing communications shall clearly state that the manager may terminate the marketing arrangements under Article 93a of Directive 2009/65/EC and Article 32a of Directive 2011/61/EU (Article 4, paragraph 3).  
- AIFMs, EuVECA managers, and EuSEF managers shall ensure that marketing communications containing specific information about an AIF do not contradict or diminish the information required by Article 23 of Directive 2011/61/EU, Article 13 of Regulation (EU) No 345/2013, or Article 14 of Regulation (EU) No 346/2013 (Article 4, paragraph 4).

- ESMA shall develop draft implementing technical standards for standard forms, templates, and procedures for publications and notifications (Article 5, paragraph 3).  
- ESMA shall publish a central database containing summaries of national requirements for marketing communications and hyperlinks to competent authority websites by 2 February 2022 (Article 6).  
- Competent authorities may require prior notification of marketing communications (Article 7) for UCITS management companies, with a requirement that notification is not a prior condition for marketing and that the authority may verify ex-post; they must inform the manager of any amendment requests within 10 working days of receipt (Article 7).  
- Competent authorities shall report to ESMA the number of requests for amendments based on ex-ante verification, ex-post verification breaches, and examples of breaches (Article 8).  
- ESMA shall submit reports to the European Parliament, Council, and Commission on marketing requirements by 31 March 2021 and every second year thereafter (Article 8).  
- Fees or charges levied by competent authorities for cross-border activities shall be consistent with the overall cost of performance of their duties (Article 9, paragraph 1). Competent authorities shall send invoices, individual payment statements, or payment instructions clearly stating means of payment and due date to the address specified in Article 93(1) of Directive 2009/65/EC or point (i) of Annex IV of Directive 2011/61/EU (Article 9, paragraph 2).

- ESMA shall publish hyperlinks to competent authority websites listing fees/charges by 2 February 2022 (Article 11) and an interactive tool for indicative fee/charge calculation by 2 February 2022 (Article 11).  
- By 2 February 2022, ESMA shall publish a central database on cross-border marketing of AIFs and UCITS listing all AIFs and UCITS marketed outside their home Member State, their managers, and the Member States where marketed (Article 12).  
- Competent authorities shall communicate quarterly to ESMA information necessary for the central database (Article 13).  
- Competent authorities shall have all necessary supervisory and investigatory powers (Article 14).  
- The Regulation amends Regulation (EU) No 345/2013, Regulation (EU) No 346/2013, and Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 to define “pre-marketing” and insert Article 4a and related provisions (Articles 15, 16, 17).  

Entry into force and application:  
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 1 August 2019. However, Articles 4(1) to (5), Article 5(1) and (2), Article 15 and Article 16 shall apply from 2 August 2021.  

The Regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.

This is a Council Decision (CFSP) under the Common Foreign and Security Policy, adopting a European Union military operation in the Mediterranean, designated EUNAVFOR MED IRINI.

(a) The instrument is a Council Decision (CFSP) with legal basis in the Treaty on European Union, specifically Articles 42(4) and 43(2) TEU.

(b) Subject matter: The operation is a military crisis management operation aimed at implementing the UN arms embargo on Libya, preventing illicit export of petroleum from Libya, assisting in capacity building and training of the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy, and disrupting the business model of human smuggling and trafficking networks. The operation’s territorial scope is the Area of Operation and Area of Interest defined in planning documents, primarily in the Mediterranean region, including high seas off the coast of Libya and relevant maritime and aerial zones. The operation is confined to tasks related to the UN arms embargo, petroleum export measures, maritime surveillance, law enforcement at sea, and human smuggling/trafficking detection. Personal scope is limited to EU-led and participating third-state personnel and operations; Union-led units and personnel are subject to international law and EU status rules. The operation does not extend to political or diplomatic missions, and Denmark is excluded from participation, implementation, and financing.

(c) Primary obligations:
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall contribute to the implementation of the UN arms embargo on Libya through aerial, satellite and maritime assets, including conducting inspections of vessels suspected of carrying arms or related materiel in violation of the embargo, seizing prohibited items, and disposing of them with port State consent, in accordance with UNSCRs 1970 (2011), 2292 (2016), 2473 (2019), and UNSCRs 2509 (2020) and 2510 (2020).
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall gather and share comprehensive, case-by-case, need-to-know information on arms trafficking, including classified information up to “SECRET UE/EU SECRET” level, in accordance with Council Decision 2013/488/EU and Article 14(9) of this Decision, handling classified data without distinction between staff based solely on operational requirements.
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall conduct monitoring and surveillance to detect illicit petroleum exports from Libya in accordance with UNSCR 2146 (2014) and subsequent resolutions (e.g., UNSCR 2509 (2020), 2510 (2020)), and may store or release such information to legitimate Libyan authorities, Member State law enforcement, and competent Union bodies.
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall assist in capacity building and training of the Libyan Coast Guard and Navy in law enforcement tasks at sea, including prevention of human smuggling and trafficking, conducted in the Area of Operation (high seas, territorial waters, or host third-state waters where authorized), and may be carried out in Member States upon invitation.
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall support disruption of human smuggling and trafficking networks through aerial patrols and information gathering, collecting and transmitting data on smuggling/trafficking relevant to security, in accordance with UNSCR 2240 (2015).
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall report to the Political and Security Committee (PSC) on all inspections, events, and related issues, and the PSC may consider subsequent measures.
- The PSC may prolong the operation unless the deployment of maritime assets produces a pull effect on migration, based on substantiated evidence from the Operations Plan.
- The operation shall be reconfirmed every four months, with reconfirmation required under Article 38 TEU.
- The EU Operation Commander and Force Commander shall be appointed and may be replaced as authorized by the PSC under Article 38 TEU.
- The PSC shall have authority to amend planning documents, including the Operations Plan, Chain of Command, Rules of Engagement, and to take decisions on appointment of commanders, subject to the Council’s retained authority over objectives and termination.
- The HR shall ensure consistency with Union external action, including development and humanitarian programs.
- The operation shall be coordinated with relevant EU and international bodies (e.g., Frontex, EUROPOL, EUROJUST, SATCEN, INTCEN, etc.), and shall host a Crime Information Cell (CIC) to collect, transmit, and process personal and operational data on arms embargo, petroleum export, and smuggling/trafficking, in accordance with applicable law (flag State law for vessel-based CIC, Union agency legal framework for staff).
- Classified and sensitive personal data shall be handled without distinction between staff based solely on operational requirements.
- The HR may release non-classified EU documents, classified information up to “CONFIDENTIEL UE/EU CONFIDENTIAL” or “RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED” levels (as defined in Decision 2013/488/EU), and EU classified information up to “RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED” to legitimate Libyan authorities, subject to PSC and HR approval, and in accordance with applicable Security of Information Agreements or other conditions.
- The HR may release EU classified information to INTERPOL, subject to INTERPOL arrangements and national central bureaux, pending agreement.
- EUNAVFOR MED IRINI shall transmit to the UN, in accordance with UNSCR 2509 (2020), information on suspected non-compliance with the UN arms embargo (per UNSCR 1970 (2011) and subsequent resolutions) and with UN measures to prevent illicit petroleum export (per UNSCR 2146 (2014) and subsequent resolutions).

(d) Key defined terms:
- “EUNAVFOR MED IRINI”: the European Union naval operation designated for the Mediterranean, as defined in Article 1.
- “Area of Operation” and “Area of Interest”: the specific maritime, aerial, and territorial zones defined in the relevant planning documents approved by the Council.
- “UN arms embargo on Libya”: the embargo established by UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011) and subsequent resolutions (e.g., 2292 (2016), 2473 (2019)).
- “UN measures to prevent illicit export of petroleum from Libya”: measures under UNSCR 2146 (2014) and subsequent resolutions (e.g., 2509 (2020), 2510 (2020)).
- “UNSC Resolution 2509 (2020)” and “UNSC Resolution 2510 (2020)”: specific UN resolutions referenced for the operation’s mandate.
- “UNSC Resolution 2292 (2016)” and “UNSC Resolution 2473 (2019)”: referenced for arms embargo implementation.
- “UNSC Resolution 2240 (2015)” (for human smuggling/trafficking): referenced for disruption task.
- “UNSC Resolution 1970 (2011)” and subsequent arms embargo resolutions: referenced for arms embargo implementation.
- “UNSC Resolution 2146 (2014)” and subsequent petroleum export measures: referenced for petroleum export task.
- “PSC” (Political and Security Committee): the EU body exercising political control and strategic direction.
- “EU Operation Commander” and “EU Force Commander”: designated personnel responsible for operational execution.
- “Area of Operation” and “Area of Interest”: defined in planning documents approved by the Council.
- “CIC” (Crime Information Cell): a coordinated body for collecting, transmitting, and processing information on arms embargo, petroleum export, and smuggling/trafficking.
- “classified information” and “personal data”: defined in accordance with Council Decision 2013/488/EU and applicable EU and national law; personal data collection is limited to specific categories (surname, maiden name, given names, aliases, date/place of birth, nationality, sex, place of residence, profession, whereabouts, driving licenses, identification documents, passport data) and is collected only with written consent from persons involved, and only for vetting purposes; no other personal data is collected or stored.
- “pull effect on migration”: a condition under which the PSC may not prolong the operation; defined as the deployment of maritime assets producing a measurable reduction in migration flows, based on substantiated evidence from the Operations Plan.
- “reconfirmation every four months”: the operation’s authorisation shall be reconfirmed every four months; the PSC may prolong the operation unless the pull effect condition is met.
- “Denmark”: excluded from participation, implementation, and financing; not bound by or subject to this Decision.

(e) Entry into force and termination:
- This Decision shall enter into force on the date of its adoption, i.e., 31 March 2020.
- The operation shall end on 31 March 2021.
- The Decision shall be repealed as from the date of closure of the EU Operation Headquarters, in accordance with the termination plans approved for EUNAVFOR MED IRINI, without prejudice to the audit and accounting procedures set out in Decision (CFSP) 2015/528.

This Council Decision (EU, Euratom) 2020/2053, adopted on 14 December 2020, is a Decision of the Council of the European Union and is based on the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), particularly Article 311 thereof, and the Treaty establishing the European Atomic Energy Community (Article 106a). It repeals Decision 2014/335/EU, Euratom, and establishes a revised system of own resources for the European Union, with a focus on simplifying the calculation of VAT-based own resources and introducing new categories based on non-recycled plastic packaging waste, carbon border adjustment mechanisms, digital levies, and other measures.

The Decision applies to the Union’s own resources system, covering the territorial, sectoral, and personal scope of the Union’s annual budget, including the allocation of own resources to cover appropriations for payments and commitments, as well as the integration of the European Development Fund. It applies from 1 January 2021.

The primary obligations established include:

- The collection and allocation of own resources as defined in Article 2, including VAT-based own resources calculated using uniform call rates (e.g., 0.30% of VAT receipts, EUR 0.80 per kilogram of non-recycled plastic packaging waste, and a uniform GNI-based call rate), with specific procedural rules for calculation, weighting, and adjustments (e.g., lump-sum reductions for Member States with GNI per capita below the EU average).
- Member States retain 25% of traditional own resources collected (as defined in Article 2(1)(a)) as collection costs.
- The total own resources allocated to cover annual appropriations for payments shall not exceed 1.40% of the sum of all Member States’ GNIs; the total annual appropriations for commitments shall not exceed 1.46% of the sum of all Member States’ GNIs.
- An orderly ratio between appropriations for payments and commitments is maintained.
- Where amendments to Regulation (EU) No 549/2013 result in significant changes in GNI, the ceilings shall be temporarily recalculated in accordance with Article 6.

This is a Regulation (EU) 2020/493 adopted by the European Parliament and the Council. Its legal basis is Article 87(2)(a) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).  

The Regulation establishes the False and Authentic Documents Online (FADO) system, replacing Council Joint Action 98/700/JHA. It applies to the FADO system, which provides electronic storage, rapid exchange, and validation of information on authentic and false documents (including forged, counterfeit, and pseudo documents) issued by Member States, the Union, and third parties (e.g., third countries, territorial entities, international organisations, and other entities subject to international law), as well as their false versions. The system is intended to support Member State authorities competent in document fraud (e.g., police, border guard, law enforcement) and other relevant actors in detecting false documents, and to provide limited access to the general public and other specified third parties.  

The Regulation’s scope is territorial (applicable to all Member States and relevant third parties as defined), sectoral (focused on document fraud, identity documents, travel, identity, residence, civil status, driving licences, vehicle licences), and personal data processing is strictly limited to security features, fraud characteristics, and pseudonymised data as required by data minimisation principles (see Article 5).  

Primary obligations include:  
- Member States and the Union must transmit information on authentic and false documents (including security features, fraud characteristics, and specimens) to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (the “Agency”) without delay (Article 1, Article 2(3)).  
- The Agency must ensure proper functioning of the FADO system, enter and maintain uniform, high-quality information, and provide support to competent Member State authorities in detecting false documents (Article 3).  
- The Commission and the Agency (as well as competent Member State authorities) must have secure, need-to-know access to the FADO system (Article 4).  
- The Agency must process personal data only as strictly necessary for operating the FADO system, applying data minimisation and pseudonymisation rules (Article 5), and must not enable identification of natural persons without additional data (Article 5).  
- Implementing acts shall define the technical architecture, specifications, verification procedures, and effective implementation date of the FADO system by the Agency (Article 6).

- “FADO system” – the False and Authentic Documents Online system described in this Regulation.

- “Personal data” – as defined under Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 (processing of personal data by the Agency under this Regulation).  
- “Pseudonymised data” – data transformed in such a way that it can no longer be used to identify a natural person, consistent with data minimisation and Article 5 requirements.  
- “Specimens” – physical or digital representations of authentic documents (e.g., specimen images) used in the FADO system.  

The Regulation repeals Council Joint Action 98/700/JHA with effect from the date of effective implementation of the FADO system by the Agency, as determined by an implementing act (Article 9(1)). Regulation (EU) 2020/672 of the Council of the European Union  
of 19 May 2020  
on the establishment of a European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency (SURE) following the COVID-19 outbreak  

(1) This Regulation is a Regulation under the legal basis of Article 122 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).  

(2) The subject matter and territorial, sectoral, or personal scope of application:  
The Regulation establishes a European instrument (the “SURE Instrument”) for temporary financial assistance to Member States experiencing severe economic disturbance caused by the COVID-19 outbreak, specifically to support short-time work schemes and similar measures for employees and self-employed persons, as well as ancillary health-related measures in the workplace. The assistance is provided solely to Member States that are not the United Kingdom, and the instrument is applicable only to Member States that have contributed to the Instrument in accordance with Article 11, and only while the exceptional circumstances of the COVID-19 outbreak continue to exist. The scope is limited to Member States affected by the pandemic and is sectoral in nature, focusing on labour market policies and related economic support measures.  

(3) Primary obligations, prohibitions, or entitlements (with reference to relevant articles):  
- A Member State may request Union financial assistance under the SURE Instrument only if its actual and possibly planned public expenditure has suddenly and severely increased as of 1 February 2020, directly due to national measures related to short-time work schemes or similar measures (including for self-employed persons) caused by the COVID-19 outbreak.  
- The financial assistance shall be granted in the form of a loan (Article 4).  
- The maximum amount of financial assistance for all Member States shall not exceed EUR 100,000,000,000 (Article 5).  
- The loan shall be disbursed in instalments (Article 7).  
- The loan shall be carried out in euros, and the loan agreement shall contain provisions set out in Article 220(5) of Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2018/1046 (Article 8).  
- The beneficiary Member State shall use the financial assistance primarily to finance its national short-time work schemes or similar measures, and, where applicable, ancillary health-related measures (Article 3).  
- The Commission shall be empowered, through a Council implementing decision, to borrow on the Union’s behalf on the most appropriate market conditions to optimise funding costs (Article 4).  
- The Commission shall consult the requesting Member State before adopting an implementing decision, verify the sudden and severe increase in public expenditure, and ensure compliance with prudential rules (Article 6).  
- The Council shall consider existing and expected needs, applying principles of equal treatment, solidarity, proportionality, and transparency (Article 6).  
- The Instrument shall not be applicable to the United Kingdom (Article 15).  
- No financial assistance shall be provided once the COVID-19 emergency has passed, unless the Council, on a proposal from the Commission, extends the period of availability where the exceptional circumstances continue to exist (Article 12, paragraph 3; Article 15).  
- The Commission shall assess every six months whether the exceptional circumstances still exist and report to the Council (Article 14).  
- Member States may contribute to the Instrument by providing irrevocable, unconditional, on-demand guarantees (Article 11).  
- The Commission may call on guarantees from Member States pro rata to their relative share of gross national income (Article 11).  
- The Commission shall inform Member States of the extent to which the available margin under the own-resources ceiling has been drawn before calling on guarantees (Article 11).  
- The Instrument shall become available only after at least 25 per cent of the maximum amount (EUR 100,000,000,000) has been contributed by Member States in accordance with the relative shares of their gross national income (Article 12).  
- The period of availability shall end on 31 December 2022, and may be extended by the Council, on a proposal from the Commission, in periods of six months each time, where the Commission concludes that the exceptional circumstances continue to exist (Article 12, paragraph 3; Article 15).  

(4) Key defined terms (as used in the text and preserved verbatim):  
- “SURE Instrument” – refers to the European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency (SURE).  
- “short-time work schemes” – public programmes allowing businesses experiencing economic difficulties to temporarily reduce employee hours, with public income support for hours not worked.  
- “self‑employed” – persons who are economically active through self‑employment, covered by similar income replacement schemes.  
- “health‑related measures” – measures aimed at reducing occupational hazards and ensuring protection of workers and self‑employed persons in the workplace (as defined in the context of the instrument).  
- “financial assistance” – the loan granted under the SURE Instrument.  
- “public expenditure” – actual and planned expenditure incurred by a Member State due to national measures related to short-time work schemes or similar measures (including health‑related measures) caused by the COVID-19 outbreak.  
- “irrevocable, unconditional and on‑demand guarantees” – guarantees provided by Member States to the Union, as defined in Article 11.  
- “contingent financial liabilities” – liabilities arising from financial operations taken by the Union, including under the balance of payments facility (as referenced in Article 11).  
- “prudential rules” – rules set out in Article 9, including limits on the share of loans to the three largest Member States, limits on annual Union borrowing, and the possibility of rolling over borrowings (Article 9).  

(5) Entry into force and transitional/sunset provisions:  
This Regulation shall enter into force on the date of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (i.e., 20 May 2020).  
The Regulation is not applicable to the United Kingdom (Article 15).

The subject matter concerns the establishment and operation of a mandatory transparency register for interest representatives—natural or legal persons, formal or informal groups, associations, or networks—engaged in activities that influence the formulation, implementation, or decision-making of EU policy or legislation, or the activities of Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies. The register is intended to ensure transparency, ethical conduct, and accountability in interest representation.

The territorial, sectoral, and personal scope applies to all signatory institutions (European Parliament, Council of the European Union, and European Commission) and to interest representatives acting on behalf of associations, networks, or public authorities (including those acting on behalf of public authorities at national or subnational level, subject to specific exclusions), as well as to Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies (other than the signatory institutions) that voluntarily choose to apply the operating principles. It does not cover activities of public authorities of Member States acting exclusively on their own behalf, activities of social partners in social dialogue, submissions in response to specific factual requests, purely private or social meetings, or activities carried out by natural persons acting solely in a personal capacity without association.

DECISION (EU) 2022/313 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL  
of 24 February 2022  

providing macro-financial assistance to Ukraine  

(1) The Union’s macro-financial assistance shall be an exceptional financial instrument of untied and undesignated balance-of-payments support, aimed at addressing Ukraine’s immediate external financing needs and supporting the implementation of policy measures designed to improve Ukraine’s balance-of-payments position in the short term and enhance economic resilience in the medium term.  

(2) The assistance shall be provided in the form of loans, with a maximum total amount of EUR 1,2 billion, to be disbursed over a period of 12 months, beginning on the first day after the entry into force of the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) referred to in Article 3(1). The assistance shall be made available subject to the conditions set out in Articles 2, 3, 4 and other relevant articles.  

(3) The Union’s macro-financial assistance shall be granted only on the condition that Ukraine respects effective democratic mechanisms, including a multi-party parliamentary system, the rule of law, and guarantees of respect for human rights (Article 2). The Commission and the European External Action Service shall monitor the fulfilment of this precondition throughout the life of the assistance.  

(4) The conditions for the assistance shall be set out in a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) negotiated by the Commission, in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 182/2011, and shall focus on structural reforms, sound public finances, efficiency, transparency, and accountability of public finance management, as well as progress in mutual market opening, rule-based and fair trade, and other priorities relevant to Union external policy (Article 3). The MOU shall include a timeframe for the implementation of these conditions.  

(5) The Union’s macro-financial assistance shall be disbursed in two equal instalments, each of which shall be a loan, with the disbursement schedule set out in the MOU. The release of the second instalment shall not occur earlier than three months after the release of the first instalment (Article 4). The release of each instalment shall be subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions:  
 (a) the precondition set out in Article 2;  
 (b) a continuous satisfactory track record of implementing a non-precautionary IMF credit arrangement;  
 (c) the satisfactory implementation of the economic policy and financial conditions agreed in the MOU.  

If any of these conditions are not met, the Commission shall temporarily suspend or cancel the disbursement of the assistance and shall inform the European Parliament and the Council of the reasons (Article 4).  

(6) The Union’s macro-financial assistance shall be made available for a period of 12 months from the date of the entry into force of the MOU (Article 1). If during this period Ukraine’s financing needs decrease fundamentally compared to initial projections, the Commission, acting under the examination procedure referred to in Article 7(2), may reduce the amount of assistance or suspend or cancel it (Article 1).  

(7) The assistance shall be provided in euro, using the same value date, and shall not involve the Union in transforming maturities, nor expose the Union to exchange, interest rate, or other commercial risks (Article 5). Where feasible and requested by Ukraine, the Commission may include an early repayment clause in the loan terms, matched by a corresponding clause in the borrowing operations (Article 5).  

(8) All costs related to the borrowing and lending operations under this Decision shall be borne by Ukraine (Article 5).  

(9) The Union’s macro-financial assistance shall be implemented under direct management by the Commission, in accordance with Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2018/1046 and Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 (Article 6). The loan agreement shall contain specific provisions, including those listed in Article 6(3), such as:  
 (a) Ukraine’s regular checks on proper use of Union financing, measures to prevent fraud, corruption and irregularities, and legal action where misappropriation occurs;  
 (b) protection of the Union’s financial interests, including measures under Council Regulations (EC, Euratom) No 2988/95, (Euratom, EC) No 2185/96, Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 883/2013, and, where applicable, Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1939;  
 (c) authorisation of the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) to conduct investigations, on-the-spot checks, digital forensic operations, and interviews;  
 (d) authorisation of the Commission (or its representatives) to carry out checks, including on-the-spot inspections;  
 (e) authorisation of the Commission and the Court of Auditors to perform audits (including operational assessments) during and after the availability period;  
 (f) provision that early repayment may be triggered if Ukraine engages in fraud, corruption, or other illegal activity detrimental to Union financial interests;  
 (g) confirmation that all Union costs related to borrowing and lending operations are borne by Ukraine.  

(10) The Commission shall regularly inform the European Parliament and the Council of developments, including disbursements, progress, and compliance with conditions (Article 1, Article 3, Article 4, Article 8).  

(11) The decision shall enter into force on the day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union (Article 9).  

(12) The decision is adopted by the European Parliament and the Council in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure (1).  

(13) The legal basis of this Decision is Article 212 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.  

(14) The decision does not create new obligations beyond those expressly set out in the operative articles; all obligations, prohibitions, and entitlements are defined in the operative articles (Articles 1–9) and related provisions.

 - “precondition” – the requirement that Ukraine respects effective democratic mechanisms, the rule of law, and guarantees of respect for human rights (Article 2).  
 - “balance-of-payments needs” – the residual external financing gap identified in Ukraine’s IMF programme and other multilateral arrangements, as referenced in Article 1.  

(16) No transitional or sunset provisions are provided; the decision applies prospectively from its entry into force.  

(17) The decision does not contain any provisions for extension, suspension, or termination other than those expressly set out in Articles 1, 4, and the conditions for reduction, suspension, or cancellation of assistance (Article 1).
